In addition, since a contamination field arising from an accident or explosion could cause human casualties, a thermal camera to detect warm bodies and image processing software to recognize human bodies could be beneficially incorporated as part of the SDF data analysis suite. A major new use case concerns recent events in northern and eastern Ukraine. During wartime, nuclear facilities and legacy nuclear sites may be inadvertently or intentionally disturbed and/or damaged [65]. In such scenarios, the US and its allies have the need to rapidly regain radiological situational awareness. SDF systems human-carried or coupled to manually or autonomously operated vehicles could benefit such missions. A significant aspect of the SDF technology is the ability to incorporate geometries obtained a priori, or to generate those geometries in situ. In war and post-detonation scenarios, it is possible that previous 3D maps are rendered erroneous due to effects of blast waves, et cetera. The ability LBNL Report #2001653 to generate in situ maps is therefore of significant value in many contamination mapping scenarios. Related to 3D map generation is the incorporation of knowledge of obstructions when generating SDF system matrices. SDF would play a role in gathering measurements to inform on the fate and transport of contaminants, and in the process, perhaps characterize the source responsible for the contaminants. Due to the time-evolving nature of the radiative source, and its spatial extent, this would benefit from a swarm of SDF platforms rather than a single one. The platforms navigation planning could also couple with probabilistic forward models of the plume to prioritize survey of areas that would most efficiently constrain the suite of plume models.
